source_text: λέπρα ἐστίν.» Ἰσχνομυθία μὲν οὖν τὸ χρῆμά ἐστιν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, καὶ οὐχ ἕτοιμος ἑλεῖν ὁ ἐπὶ τοῖσδε λόγος. Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ οἶμαι συνενεγκόντα τὸν νοῦν, ὡς ἐν ὀλίγοις εἰπεῖν, τὸ τί ἂν βούλοιτο δηλοῦν ὁ νόμος. Προεξηγήσομαι δὲ τέως τοῦ πάθους τὴν διαφοράν. Λέπρα μὲν οὖν τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις σώμασι παγχάλεπόν ἐστι πάθος, καὶ δυσδιάφυκτον καὶ βορόν· συμβαίνει δὲ κατὰ νέκρωσιν. Κοιλαίνεται μὲν γὰρ τὸ τραῦμα εὐθὺς, δαπανωμένου τοῦ δέρματος, καὶ εἰς βάθος ἀεὶ συνιζάνοντος· ἅτε δὴ, καὶ διερπούσης ἀεὶ πρὸς τὸ κάτω τῆς φθορᾶς. Ὅθεν τοι, καθάπερ ἐγῷμαι, καὶ ἡ θρὶξ ἐπανθοῦσα τοῖς τόποις μαραινομένη, καταλευκαίνεται, καὶ οἱονεί τι φυτὸν τῇ ὑποκειμένῃ συγκαταφθείρεται γῇ. Λέπρα μὲν οὖν τὸ τοιόνδε πάθος. Λεύκη δὲ πάλιν, ἀῤῥώστημα σαρκικὸν τῇ λέπρᾳ προσεοικὸς, πλὴν οὐκ ἐνίησι τὸ λυποῦν εἰς βάθος, οὔτε μὴν εἰσπέμπει τοῖς ἔσω τῆς νόσου τὴν αἴσθησιν, ἐπινήχεται δὲ ὥσπερ ἄκρῳ τε, καὶ μόλις ἐπανθοῦσα τῷ σώματι, καὶ οὐδὲ τρίχα μεθίστησιν εἰς τὸ λευκὸν, οὔτε μὴν ἀκαθέκτως εὐρύνεται, ἀλλ' ὀλίγοις κομιδῇ τοῖς ἐπικουρήμασιν εὐκόλως ἀνασειράζεται, καὶ ὑπονοστεῖ πρὸς ὑγιὲς ἡ ἐπανθοῦσα σάρξ. Οὐκοῦν ἡ μὲν λέπρα, νέκρωσις ὁμολογουμένη, ἐν ὑποψίαις δέ πως τῆς λέπρας ἡ λεύκη, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατὰ ἀλήθειαν, λέπρα καὶ νέκρωσις. Καταψηφίζεται τοίνυν ὁ νόμος τοῦ λεπροῦ τὸ ἀκάθαρτον, ὡς ἤδη παθόντος τὴν νέκρωσιν. Ἀνίησι δὲ τοῦ ἐγκλήματος, τὸν λεύκην ἠῤῥωστηκότα, ὡς ἐν ὑποψίαις μὲν γεγονότα τοῦ λεπρᾷν, οὐ μὴν ἔτι καὶ λελεπρωμένον. Τοιγάρτοι, φησὶν, εἰ γένοιτο οὐλὴ σημασίας, καὶ ἁφὴ λέπρας, καὶ κοιλοτέρα ἡ ὄψις τοῦ δέρματος, καὶ μὴν καὶ τριχὸς εἰς λευκότητα μεταβολὴ, συναποθνησκούσης τάχα που τῇ ὑποκειμένῃ σαρκὶ, λέπρα δὴ πάντως ἔσται. Ἕρπει γὰρ εἰς βάθος ἡ νέκρωσις. Εἰ δὲ δὴ γένοιτό τις λεύκη σημασίας, δίχα κοιλότητος τῆς ἐν δέρματι, καὶ τριχὸς εἰς λευκότητα μεταβολῆς, δοκιμαζέσθω, φησὶ, παρὰ τοῦ ἱερέως, καὶ ἀφοριζέσθω δεύτερον· τὸ ἀπεικὸς γὰρ οὐδὲν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὴ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἡ παράτασις, τὸ ἀῤῥώστημα βασανίζουσα, παραδείξειεν ἂν ἔσθ' ὅτε τοῖς ἐρευνῶσι τὸ ἀκριβές. Ἡ μὲν γὰρ θρὶξ ὑπομένει τὸ ἑτερόχρουν, κοιλαινομένου τοῦ δέρματος, μετακεχώρηκε δὲ πρὸς λέπραν ἡ λεύκη. Οὐδενὸς δὲ τούτων γεγονότος, «Ἀνείσθω, φησὶ, τῆς αἰτίας.» Οὐ γάρ τοι λέπρα τὸ πάθος, ἀλλὰ τὸ λέπρᾳ προσεοικὸς, καὶ ἀγχοῦ δὴ μάλα, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ἡ λεύκη. Ὁ μὲν οὖν ἐν προχείρῳ λόγος, καὶ ἡ τοῦ πράγματος διασάφησις ἀποχρῶσαν ἔχει τὴν παράθεσιν. Ἀλλὰ φέρε λέγωμεν τὰ πνευματικὰ, καὶ τῶν εἰς νοῦν τε καὶ κεκρυμμένων ἐννοιῶν ἁπτώμεθα. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ὡς καλὸν τὸ χρῆμα καὶ ὀνησιφόρον. {ΚΥΡ.} Χρὴ τοίνυν ἡμᾶς τοὺς ἐν Χριστῷ ζωοποιουμένους, ζωοποίησιν δέ φημι τὴν πνευματικὴν, νεκρῶν ἔργων ἀποφοιτᾷν, καὶ ὡς ἀπωτάτω χωρεῖν, εἶεν δ' ἂν, οἶμαι, ταυτὶ, τὰ δι' ὧν ἂν γένοιτο κατανεκροῦσθαι ψυχὴν, καὶ ἀποψύχεσθαι νοῦν, ἀχαλίνως ἐκνενευκότα πρὸς τὰ σαρκός τε καὶ κόσμου. Εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθὲς, ὡς ὁ εἰς τὴν σάρκα σπείρων, ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς θερίσει φθοράν· καὶ οἱ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶντες
pass_a_gloss: [§17 PG 68.980] End of Lev 13 quotation: λέπρα ἐστίν 'it is leprosy'. Cyril: ἰσχνομυθία (fine-drawn, minute account) is the matter, O Palladius, and not easy to seize (οὐχ ἕτοιμος ἑλεῖν) is the account on these things. Necessary, I think, having gathered the mind (συνενεγκόντα τὸν νοῦν), to say in few words what the law wishes to show (δηλοῦν). I will first explain (προεξηγήσομαι) the difference (διαφορά) of the affliction (πάθος). Leprosy (λέπρα) for human bodies is an altogether grievous affliction (παγχάλεπον), hard to escape (δυσδιάφυκτον) and devouring (βορόν); it happens by way of deadening (κατὰ νέκρωσιν). The wound is hollowed (κοιλαίνεται) at once, the skin being consumed (δαπανωμένου) and always sinking into depth (εἰς βάθος συνιζάνοντος), since the corruption (φθορά) always creeps (διερπούσης) downward. Hence, as I think, the hair blooming on the places, withering (μαραινομένη), whitens (καταλευκαίνεται), and like a plant perishes with (συγκαταφθείρεται) the underlying earth. Leprosy, then, is such an affliction. Leukē (λεύκη, white patch/vitiligo-like ailment) again: a fleshly sickness (ἀῤῥώστημα σαρκικόν) resembling (προσεοικός) leprosy, except it does not send the hurt into depth, nor send the sensation (αἴσθησις) of the disease to the inward parts, but floats (ἐπινήχεται) as on the surface, barely blooming (ἐπανθοῦσα) on the body, and does not change hair to white, nor widen uncontrollably (ἀκαθέκτως εὐρύνεται), but with very few remedies (ἐπικουρήμασιν) is easily reined back (ἀνασειράζεται), and the blooming flesh returns (ὑπονοστεῖ) to health (ὑγιές). So leprosy is admitted deadening (νέκρωσις ὁμολογουμένη); leukē is under suspicions (ἐν ὑποψίαις) of leprosy, yet not in truth the same, leprosy and deadening. The law condemns (καταψηφίζεται) the uncleanness of the leper as already having suffered the deadening; it releases (ἀνίησι) from the charge (ἔγκλημα) the one sick with leukē, as having come under suspicion of being leprous, not yet having been made leprous (λελεπρωμένον). Therefore, he says, if there should be a scar of a mark (οὐλὴ σημασίας) and touch/sore of leprosy (ἁφὴ λέπρας) and the appearance (ὄψις) of the skin more hollow, and indeed change of hair to whiteness, the hair perhaps dying with (συναποθνησκούσης) the underlying flesh, it will be leprosy altogether; for deadening creeps (ἕρπει) into depth. If there should be a leukē of a mark without hollowness in the skin and change of hair to whiteness, let it be tested (δοκιμαζέσθω) by the priest and let it be set apart (ἀφοριζέσθω) a second time; nothing unlikely that the very prolongation (παράτασις) of the days, testing (βασανίζουσα) the sickness, would show at times to the searchers the exact truth (τὸ ἀκριβές). For [in one case] the hair endures the other colour (ἑτερόχρουν), the skin being hollowed, and the leukē has moved over (μετακεχώρηκε) to leprosy. None of these having happened, 'let him be released,' he says, 'from the charge (αἰτία).' For the affliction is not leprosy, but what resembles leprosy and is very near (ἀγχοῦ), that is, leukē. The ready-to-hand account (ὁ ἐν προχείρῳ λόγος) and the clarification (διασάφησις) of the thing have sufficient setting-out (ἀποχρῶσαν παράθεσιν). But come, let us say the spiritual things (τὰ πνευματικά) and touch the ideas that are for the mind and hidden (κεκρυμμένων ἐννοιῶν). Palladius: How fine the thing and profit-bringing (ὀνησιφόρον). Cyril: We who are being made alive (ζωοποιουμένους) in Christ, and I mean spiritual making-alive (ζωοποίησις), must depart (ἀποφοιτᾶν) from dead works (νεκρῶν ἔργων) and go as far away as possible; these would be, I think, the things through which it happens that soul is deadened (κατανεκροῦσθαι) and mind grows cold/faints (ἀποψύχεσθαι), having bent away unbridled (ἀχαλίνως ἐκνενευκότα) to the things of flesh and world. For if it is true that the one sowing into the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh (Gal 6:8), and those living according to the flesh (κατὰ σάρκα ζῶντες) [continues in §18].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …it is leprosy.’ (Leviticus 13:8) The matter, Palladius, turns on fine distinctions, and the account of these things is not easy to grasp. Yet I think I must gather my mind and say in a few words what the law means to show. But first I will explain how the conditions differ. Leprosy is a most grievous disease of human bodies, hard to escape and devouring, and it comes about by a deadening. The sore is hollowed out at once, as the skin is consumed and keeps sinking deeper, since the corruption always creeps downward. That, I think, is why the hair growing on those places withers and turns white, and like a plant it perishes along with the soil beneath it. Such, then, is leprosy. The white patch, on the other hand, is a bodily ailment that resembles leprosy, except that it does not drive the harm deep or send the feeling of the disease into the parts within. It floats, as it were, on the surface and barely blooms on the body. It does not turn the hair white, nor does it spread beyond control; with very few remedies it is easily reined in, and the flesh where it broke out returns to health. So leprosy is an undoubted deadness, while the white patch raises some suspicion of leprosy but is not in truth the same thing, that is, leprosy and deadness. The law therefore condemns the leper as unclean, since he has already suffered deadness; but it acquits of the charge the one sick with the white patch, since he has come under suspicion of leprosy but is not actually leprous. This is why it says that if there is a scar with a mark, and a leprous sore, and the skin looks hollowed, and the hair also changes to white, dying, it may be, together with the flesh beneath it, then it will certainly be leprosy (Leviticus 13:2–3); for the deadness creeps deep. But if there is a white patch with a mark, without any hollowing of the skin and without the hair changing to white, let it be tested, it says, by the priest, and let the man be set apart a second time (Leviticus 13:4–5). For it is not unlikely that the passing of the days itself, putting the ailment to the test, may sometimes show the exact truth to those who examine it. In one case the hair takes on another color as the skin hollows, and the white patch has turned into leprosy. But if none of these things has happened, ‘let him be released,’ it says, ‘from the charge’ (Leviticus 13:6). For the condition is not leprosy, but something that resembles leprosy and comes very close to it, namely the white patch. The plain sense, then, and the explanation of the matter have been set out well enough. But come, let us speak of the spiritual meaning and lay hold of the ideas that are hidden and grasped by the mind.
Palladius: How fine and helpful that is!

Cyril: We who are being made alive in Christ (and by making alive I mean the spiritual kind) must depart from dead works (Hebrews 9:14) and go as far from them as we can. These, I think, would be the works through which the soul is put to death and the mind grows cold, when it has turned without restraint toward the things of the flesh and of the world.
